documents.unit: Office of Research and Innovation, AI (ORAI)
documents.title: AI Guidelines & Principles (University Guidelines and Academic Integrity)
documents.summary: The university AI office page says there is no single university-wide AI policy, so use of AI in coursework falls under the Code of Academic Integrity. Students may use AI only with explicit instructor approval, instructors are urged to put expectations in the syllabus, and sample Red-Yellow-Green language is offered.
documents.stance_why: The page says students 'may only use AI tools for class assignments if your instructor has explicitly approved their use' and that unapproved use 'may violate the Code of Academic Integrity'. AI is banned unless permitted, which is restrict, even though instructors choose whether to permit; there are no stated tiers on this page itself.

units.why: The page says AI use in coursework is 'guided by the Code of Academic Integrity, which prohibits all forms of academic dishonesty' including 'submitting AI-generated work as your own without permission'. I typed it P36 because it classifies unauthorized AI work as academic dishonesty under the Code; P19 fits less well because the point is the integrity classification.
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated work as your own without permission

units.why: The passage states 'there is currently no single, university-wide policy specific to AI', which leaves the rule to the Code and to instructors. P04 is the nearest type since the decision is pushed down to instructors.
units.anchor: no single, university-wide policy specific to AI
units.policy: The University of Arizona currently has no single, university-wide policy specific to AI.
units.fit_note: The unit states that no university-wide AI policy exists; P04 is about instructors setting the rule, which is only implied.

units.why: Instructors are 'encouraged to set clear expectations in their course materials', a recommendation to state AI expectations in course documents, so P09 with modality should.
units.anchor: instructors are encouraged to set clear expectations in their course materials

units.why: Students 'may only use AI tools for class assignments if your instructor has explicitly approved their use', which sets what applies without explicit permission. I chose P06 over P01 because the ban lifts when the instructor approves, so it is default-deny rather than a flat prohibition.
units.anchor: You may only use AI tools for class assignments if your instructor has explicitly approved

units.why: Unpermitted AI use 'may violate the Code of Academic Integrity and could be treated as academic misconduct', which classifies misuse as misconduct handled by the integrity process (P36).
units.anchor: Using AI without permission may violate the Code of Academic Integrity

units.why: Instructors are told to 'clearly communicate your expectations for AI use in your syllabus', the syllabus-statement recommendation (P09).
units.anchor: clearly communicate your expectations for AI use in your syllabus

units.why: The page offers 'sample syllabus language based on a Red-Yellow-Green model' with named levels (prohibited, allowed with permission, encouraged), so it names explicit tiers of AI use (P05).
units.anchor: sample syllabus language based on a Red-Yellow-Green model
units.policy: The university offers sample syllabus language based on a Red-Yellow-Green model, which outlines whether AI is prohibited, allowed with permission, or actively encouraged.

units.why: The page says 'many colleges and departments have developed additional guidance' beyond the institution-wide principles, which lets units add their own AI guidance (P85).
units.anchor: many colleges and departments have developed additional guidance tailored to the unique needs of their
units.policy: Many colleges and departments have developed additional guidance tailored to the unique needs of their disciplines.

units.why: The preamble says the university 'champions practices that are legally sound, ethically grounded, and academically rigorous', an institution-level statement of principles for AI, so P56.
units.anchor: champions practices that are legally sound, ethically grounded, and academically rigorous

documents.unit: UCATT (Center for Assessment, Teaching, and Technology)
documents.title: Instructor AI Policy Guide
documents.summary: UCATT's guide tells every instructor to write a course AI policy and offers three syllabus templates (permitted, sometimes permitted, never permitted). It adds communication practices, recommends against AI detectors, recommends university-licensed tools, and advises handling violations through conversation.
documents.stance_why: The guide opens 'Instructors determine their own course AI rules' and offers 'three policy options' with templates, so the document sets no stance itself and lists tiers; it is delegates.

units.why: The page opens with 'Instructors determine their own course AI rules', which leaves whether AI is allowed to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: Instructors determine their own course AI rules.

units.why: Every course 'needs an AI policy' and instructors 'should communicate to students what is—and is not—allowed and why', a duty to state AI expectations (P09). P66 also touches 'why', but the main demand is having a stated policy.
units.anchor: communicate to students what is—and is not—allowed and why

units.why: The guide tells instructors to use 'your syllabus and Brightspace course site to communicate expectations from the start', which places the AI statement in specified channels (P09).
units.anchor: Use your syllabus and Brightspace course site to communicate expectations from the start.

units.why: The guide says it is 'highly recommended to limit AI use to tools with U of A subscriptions' and names them, which is use of university-licensed tools (P92) rather than a single course tool (P17).
units.anchor: It is highly recommended to limit AI use to tools with U of A subscriptions
units.policy: It is highly recommended to limit AI use to tools with U of A subscriptions, including U of A GenAI, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini or Gemini Notebook, and Adobe tools with AI features.

units.why: Users should log in with U of A credentials 'to ensure data protection', so the rule protects data by using vetted accounts (P50).
units.anchor: using your U of A accounts to ensure data protection

units.why: Instructors are told to 'decide to what extent students may use AI in your course' using three options, so the extent of AI use is set per course (P04).
units.anchor: Decide to what extent students may use AI in your course

units.why: The guide offers three named policy options (permitted, sometimes permitted, never permitted) with templates, which is an explicit set of tiers (P05).
units.anchor: review the three policy options below
units.policy: Instructors choose among three policy options: AI is permitted, AI is sometimes permitted, and AI is never permitted.

units.why: Option 1 means 'you are allowing students to use GenAI for any and all of their coursework', an open permit-by-default option (P02).
units.anchor: you are allowing students to use GenAI for any and all of their coursework

units.why: Under the open option instructors 'may even be requiring it for some assignments', which is AI required for coursework (P79).
units.anchor: may even be requiring it for some assignments

units.why: The permitted template says 'You may use GenAI tools; however, you are responsible for the quality of all work submitted for grading'. I coded it P29 because the unit's condition is ownership of submitted work; the permit itself is already coded as P02.
units.anchor: You may use GenAI tools; however, you are responsible for the quality of all work

units.why: Students are responsible for 'human oversight and evaluation of AI-generated suggestions', i.e. they must check AI output (P31).
units.anchor: including human oversight and evaluation of AI-generated suggestions

units.why: 'Any AI support must be acknowledged per assignment expectations' requires disclosure with the submission (P24).
units.anchor: Any AI support must be acknowledged per assignment expectations.

units.why: Failing to acknowledge AI 'may be considered a violation of the Code of Academic Integrity', so nondisclosure is itself the violation (P28).
units.anchor: A lack of acknowledgment or disclosure of AI use may be considered a violation of

units.why: The template acknowledgment statement asks for the AI system, the specific use, and 'Prompts used included [share link or copy-and-paste prompt]', which is the tool-and-prompt citation (P25).
units.anchor: Prompts used included [share link or copy-and-paste prompt]
units.policy: The acknowledgment statement names the AI system, describes the specific use, and shares the prompts used by link or copy-and-paste.

units.why: The template tells students in doubt about AI use to 'please contact me', which is the ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: If you are in doubt as to whether you are misusing AI tools in this

units.why: Option 2 means 'you are allowing AI for tasks such as for brainstorming, structuring, idea generation, and editing'. I chose P15 as the lead use; editing is P91 and is only partly captured.
units.anchor: you are allowing AI for tasks such as for brainstorming, structuring, idea generation, and editing
units.fit_note: The unit lists several permitted uses (brainstorming, structuring, idea generation, editing) in one phrase; P15 covers only brainstorming and idea generation.

units.why: The guide asks instructors 'Will you specify allowed uses generally or per assignment?', which makes the level of the rule an instructor choice (P04).
units.anchor: Will you specify allowed uses generally or per assignment?

units.why: Instructors are prompted to ask how they and their students 'learn from each other about what is — and is not — ethical, possible, and helpful', which is discussing the AI rules with students (P66).
units.anchor: how might you and your students learn from each other about what is

units.why: The sometimes-permitted template says 'GenAI tools may be used for some coursework', with the instructor listing allowed and forbidden tasks, so the rule is set per assignment (P04).
units.anchor: GenAI tools may be used for

units.why: The sometimes-permitted template requires that AI support 'must be acknowledged' to avoid violating the Code, which is disclosure (P24). It is a separate template from Option 1, so I code it again.
units.anchor: AI support must be acknowledged per assignment expectations so as not to violate the

units.why: Option 3 means 'you are requiring that students complete coursework entirely without GenAI assistance', a ban on AI for the work (P01).
units.anchor: you are requiring that students complete coursework entirely without GenAI assistance

units.why: Instructors who ban AI are warned that AI is 'embedded in many of our daily online activities' and must 'be clear about what you mean by "AI"', i.e. define the scope (P61). It does not exempt the features, so not P100.
units.anchor: AI is embedded in many of our daily online activities
units.policy: AI is embedded in many daily online activities (spell check, Google summaries, closed captioning), so instructors who disallow AI must be clear about what they mean by AI and the boundaries they set.

units.why: Instructors using a no-AI policy should 'be specific about what tools are or are not allowed', which asks for explicit statement of expectations (P09).
units.anchor: Be specific about what tools are or are not allowed

units.why: Under the no-AI option 'Suspected violations addressed per Code of Academic Integrity', so misuse goes through integrity processes (P36).
units.anchor: Suspected violations addressed per Code of Academic Integrity

units.why: The guide asks instructors 'How can you revise assignments to discourage misuse?', redesigning assignments around AI (P35).
units.anchor: How can you revise assignments to discourage misuse?

units.why: The note says 'AI detection software is not reliable and can lead to false accusations', so detectors should not be relied on (P39).
units.anchor: AI detection software is not reliable and can lead to false accusations.

units.why: The never-permitted template explains the course 'is designed to build your original thinking, writing, and problem-solving skills, and using GenAI to replace this work would interfere with your learning', a skill-building rationale (P41).
units.anchor: using GenAI tools to replace this work would interfere with your learning

units.why: The template says 'using GenAI to complete graded assignments in this course will be considered a violation', banning AI-completed submitted work. I chose P19 over P36 because the sentence defines the forbidden act; the violation label is the consequence.
units.anchor: using GenAI to complete graded assignments in this course will be considered a violation

units.why: Instructors are asked 'How will you explain policy benefits for student learning', i.e. give students the reasons behind the rule (P66).
units.anchor: How will you explain policy benefits for student learning, personal, and professional development?

units.why: Instructors are asked whether they have 'created opportunities for students to ask questions and have discussions about AI', discussing the AI rules with students (P66).
units.anchor: Have you created opportunities for students to ask questions and have discussions about AI

units.why: The guide asks 'Will you need to adjust instructions, assignments, or assessments?', which is redesigning work around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Will you need to adjust instructions, assignments, or assessments?

units.why: Instructors decide 'what specific information should students provide when acknowledging AI use, and how much detail is required', which sets the detail of a disclosure (P25).
units.anchor: What specific information should students provide when acknowledging AI use

units.why: For violations the guide recommends 'a tiered approach that begins with a direct conversation with the student', i.e. talk first before escalating (P57).
units.anchor: We recommend a tiered approach that begins with a direct conversation with the student.

units.why: The guide says 'AI detection software is not recommended' because the tools are 'unreliable and biased', so instructors should not rely on detectors (P39).
units.anchor: AI detection software is not recommended

units.why: 'Communicate your AI policy early and often' in the syllabus, start module and assignment instructions is about stating expectations (P09).
units.anchor: Communicate your AI policy early and often.

units.why: Instructors should 'make time for questions and discussion about AI and academic integrity', discussing the rules with students (P66).
units.anchor: Make time for questions and discussion about AI and academic integrity

units.why: The guide says to 'center your policy on learning': allowed or prohibited uses 'should reflect the kinds of thinking students need to do for themselves', tying AI decisions to learning goals (P83).
units.anchor: The AI uses you allow or prohibit should reflect the kinds of thinking students need

units.why: 'Be transparent about your own use of GenAI. Acknowledge when and how you use it' is instructor disclosure of AI use (P47).
units.anchor: Be transparent about your own use of GenAI.

units.why: The guide says to 'approach violations as learning opportunities' and resolve many through conversation, an educative response to misuse (P68).
units.anchor: Approach violations as learning opportunities.

units.why: Instructors should 'give students notice if you intend to report a violation and document your conversations', a procedural step in reporting (P81).
units.anchor: Give students notice if you intend to report a violation and document your conversations.

units.why: Instructors should 'have a plan to address suspected policy violations' and 'act promptly', procedural readiness for handling misuse. P81 is the nearest type but this is preparation rather than reporting steps.
units.anchor: Have a plan to address suspected policy violations.
units.fit_note: The unit asks instructors to prepare a plan and act promptly; P81 is about the steps of formal reporting.

units.why: 'Be clear and compassionate. Clearly explain the questionable behavior while maintaining a supportive approach' favors a supportive response over a punitive one (P68).
units.anchor: Clearly explain the questionable behavior while maintaining a supportive approach.

units.why: The page offers help for instructors writing their AI statement ('Need help with your AI policy syllabus statement?'), which is faculty support (P63).
units.anchor: Need help with your AI policy syllabus statement?

documents.summary: This 2023 UCATT guidance asks instructors to include an AI syllabus statement and discuss it with students. It lists issues to weigh (learning goals, integrity, equity, privacy, bias, IP, workload), gives three sample statements, covers how to cite AI, and sets conditions for AI detection.
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'all courses should include at least a syllabus statement' and gives three sample statements ('NOT allowed', 'IS permitted or encouraged', 'allowed for certain purposes'), leaving the choice to each instructor, so delegates with tiers.

units.why: Because the catalog's 'product of independent effort' phrase 'can be interpreted differently', 'instructors should also include a statement specifically addressing course policy on the use of generative AI and discuss this policy with students', an AI syllabus statement duty (P09).

units.why: The required catalog syllabus policy says 'graded work/exercises must be the product of independent effort unless otherwise instructed'. It never mentions AI, so it is the existing baseline of student ownership of submitted work (P29).
units.anchor: graded work/exercises must be the product of independent effortunless otherwise instructed

units.why: The guide notes 'Students will potentially face different policies in different courses/assignments in regard to the use of generative AI', so one course's rule does not carry over (P11).
units.anchor: Students will potentially face different policies in different courses/assignments

units.anchor: It isextremely important to be direct and specific about course policies concerning AI.

documents.title: Academic Integrity at the College of Information Science
documents.summary: The College of Information Science integrity page lists AI generation of text or code as prohibited in every course unless the instructor gives written permission. It also sets student duties to learn each course's rules, instructor duties for syllabi, tool use in investigations, and consequences and rights in violation cases.

AI is banned unless explicitly permitted, so restrict.

units.why: The listed practices are 'PROHIBITED practices in every course, unless a given course instructor has specifically written instructions or permission to do otherwise', a default-deny fallback (P06).
units.anchor: PROHIBITED practices in every course, unless a given course instructor has

units.anchor: Generating and submitting, in whole or in part, text or code through Artificial Intelligence such

units.why: Instructors 'can and will occasionally require or permit' the listed practices (which include AI generation), so the instructor can lift the default (P04).
units.anchor: instructors can and will occasionally require or permit students to use practices in the list

units.why: When practices are required or permitted 'clear written instructions will specify the tools allowed or required, so students can be certain', a duty to state AI expectations (P09).
units.anchor: clear written instructions will specify the tools allowed or required

units.why: 'Students can use ChatGPT for an assignment if they have unambiguous written documentation from the course or instructor', a per-assignment permission with written proof (P04).
units.anchor: students can use ChatGPT for an assignment if they have unambiguous written documentation

units.why: 'It is up to each student to learn the requirements around composition, collaboration, and reuse for each College of Information Science course', students must find and follow each course's rules (P78).
units.anchor: it is up to each student to learn the requirements around composition, collaboration, and reuse

units.why: Students should learn 'How can I get help, including from sources other than course instructors, if I am having trouble completing work without violating course policies?', pointing them to human help (P72).
units.anchor: How can I get help, including from sources other than course instructors

units.why: The policy says tools can 'simulate learning and generate assessments, but this simulation replaces the valuable acts of practice and learning for the student', a skill-building rationale (P41).
units.anchor: this simulation replaces the valuable acts of practice and learning for the student

units.why: Using tools in place of required work 'risks compromising the quality of work employers expect from our program graduates', limiting tools for professional readiness (P94).
units.anchor: risks compromising the quality of work employers expect from our program graduates

units.why: Use of tools in place of required work 'hurts other students in our programs', a fairness argument (P95) rather than a skill-building one (P41).
units.anchor: which hurts other students in our programs

units.why: Instructors are expected to help students avoid violations 'by providing information on requirements and rules in syllabi, and documenting in course assignment instructions when reuse, collaboration, and assistive tool use is permitted or required' (P09).
units.anchor: providing information on requirements and rules in syllabi

units.why: Instructors must give 'unambiguous written instructions when tools prohibited in some courses are allowed in others', recognising that rules differ between courses (P11).
units.anchor: unambiguous written instructions when tools prohibited in some courses are allowed in others

units.why: Instructors 'should also remain cognizant of technological advances, modifying or and replacing assignments periodically', redesigning assignments in response to technology (P35).
units.anchor: modifying or and replacing assignments periodically

units.why: Instructors are 'expected to provide students guidelines around permitted reuse, tool use, and collaboration, including citation formats'. P09 is the nearest type; citation formats are partly P24.
units.anchor: guidelines around permitted reuse, tool use, and collaboration, including citation formats
units.fit_note: The unit also asks instructors to provide citation formats for tool use, which is partly P24.

units.why: Instructors 'have the right to deploy tools to assist in investigating plagiarism violations, such as TurnItIn, GPTZero, Stanford MOSS', using similarity and AI-detection tools (P40).
units.anchor: Instructors have the right to deploy tools to assist in investigating plagiarism violations

units.why: Instructors may investigate 'including partnering with platforms where suspected violations occur, to learn non-public information about the identities of users', gathering evidence of misuse (P40).
units.anchor: partnering with platforms where suspected violations occur

units.why: Instructors 'are expected to meet with students to discuss known violations of academic integrity', talking with the student (P57).
units.anchor: Instructors are expected to meet with students to discuss known violations

units.why: Instructors are expected 'to report violations of academic integrity to the Dean of Students', a formal reporting step (P81).
units.anchor: report violations of academic integrity to the Dean of Students

units.why: 'Faculty are expected to report all known violations of academic integrity' is a reporting duty (P81). It repeats the earlier reporting expectation in wording but is a separate stated rule.
units.anchor: Faculty are expected to report all known violations of academic integrity.

units.why: Instructors 'may withhold or deny credit for a submitted assignment that does not meet assignment requirements ... without providing proof', provided it is not treated as an integrity violation. No type covers non-misconduct grading remedies, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: instructors may withhold or deny credit for a submitted assignment that does not meet assignment
units.uncovered_note: Instructors may deny credit for work that fails assignment requirements without proof or a meeting, as long as it is not handled as a violation.

units.why: Instructors 'must give the student 15 days from notification of a violation to respond and arrange a conference', a right to respond (P64).
units.anchor: Instructors must give the student 15 days from notification of a violation to respond

units.why: Instructors should 'refrain from imposing sanctions or determining consequences until the student has expressed their perspective on the situation', fairness for accused students (P64).
units.anchor: refrain from imposing sanctions or determining consequences until the student has expressed their perspective

units.why: 'Students have the right to a conference with an Instructor during the process by which an instructor reports them to the Dean of Students', a right to respond (P64).
units.anchor: Students have the right to a conference with an Instructor during the process

units.why: Instructors 'are required to keep information about the case confidential with the exception of internal personnel with legitimate educational interests'. Case confidentiality fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Instructors are required to keep information about the case confidential
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must keep integrity-case information confidential except for personnel with a legitimate educational interest.

units.why: 'Consequences of first offenses can include failed assignments, failed courses, notations on student records, compulsory workshops' lists concrete penalties (P37).
units.anchor: Consequences of first offenses can include failed assignments, failed courses

units.why: Repeated violations can bring 'dismissal from a student's College of Information Science academic program and revoking a student's degree', concrete escalating penalties (P37).
units.anchor: dismissal from a student's College of Information Science academic program and revoking a student's degree

units.why: The policy 'encourage[s] students who commit violations or are thinking of doing so to seek help instead, and make better decisions in the future', a supportive response (P68).
units.anchor: We encourage students who commit violations or are thinking of doing so to seek help

units.why: 'Instructors should inform students on how to find help with assignments, including and in addition to direct help from instructors', human help beyond the instructor (P72).
units.anchor: Instructors should inform students on how to find help with assignments

units.why: 'Policy approved by faculty vote, April 2023' states how and when the college policy was adopted (P84).
units.anchor: Policy approved by faculty vote, April 2023.

notes: Document arizona-infosci-academic-integrity-pdf (screen=include) was not coded: its saved text (v2-arizona-infosci-pdf.txt) is a '404 Page Not Found' page from the College of Information Science site, and a refetch also returned the 404 page. The HTML page of the same policy (arizona-infosci-academic-integrity) is coded. The collect file should be rechecked or the PDF re-collected. Units coded as UNCOVERED: AI summarising of readings banned; instructor workload burden; disclosure of detector use to students; case confidentiality; denying credit for unmet requirements without a misconduct charge.
